sunday.themeNote: Every reading this week circles back to one idea: we have all been forgiven far more than we could ever repay, and that gift is meant to flow outward. Sirach warns that holding onto anger blocks us from receiving healing. Paul reminds us that our whole life belongs to a God who is endlessly merciful. And Jesus makes it vivid with a story about a man who forgot what it felt like to be let off the hook.

readings.label: First Reading
readings.fullText:
Wrath and anger are hateful things,
yet the sinner hugs them tight.
The vengeful will suffer the LORD’s vengeance,
for he remembers their sins in detail.
Forgive your neighbor’s injustice;
then when you pray, your own sins will be forgiven.
Could anyone nourish anger against another
and expect healing from the LORD?
Could anyone refuse mercy to another like himself,
can he seek pardon for his own sins?
If one who is but flesh cherishes wrath,
who will forgive his sins?
Remember your last days, set enmity aside;
remember death and decay, and cease from sin!
Think of the commandments, hate not your neighbor;
remember the Most High’s covenant, and overlook faults.
readings.summary: The book of Sirach is an ancient collection of wisdom for everyday life. This passage is blunt: anger and the desire for payback are poisonous, and holding onto them keeps us from being whole. If we want God to forgive us, we have to be willing to forgive the people around us. Thinking about our own limits and our own need for mercy is what opens the door.

reflection.reflection: God offers us healing, but holding a grudge can quietly block it. Letting go of resentment is not about excusing what happened. It is about freeing ourselves to receive what God is already offering.
reflection.question: Is there someone in your life right now, maybe a family member, a coworker, or an old friend, whose name comes to mind when you think about a hurt you are still carrying?

readings.label: Responsorial Psalm
readings.fullText:
R. (8) The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
Bless the LORD, O my soul;
and all my being, bless his holy name.
Bless the LORD, O my soul,
and forget not all his benefits.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
He pardons all your iniquities,
heals all your ills.
He redeems your life from destruction,
crowns you with kindness and compassion.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
He will not always chide,
nor does he keep his wrath forever.
Not according to our sins does he deal with us,
nor does he requite us according to our crimes.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
For as the heavens are high above the earth,
so surpassing is his kindness toward those who fear him.
As far as the east is from the west,
so far has he put our transgressions from us.
R. The Lord is kind and merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.
readings.summary: Psalm 103 is a song of praise for a God who does not treat us the way our mistakes deserve. God pardons, heals, and redeems. The image of sins removed as far as east is from west paints a picture of total, lasting forgiveness. The response we are invited to sing together sums it up: God is kind, merciful, slow to anger, and rich in compassion.

reflection.reflection: God does not keep a running tally of everything we get wrong. That kind of radical patience is what we are being invited to receive and then pass along to the people we see every day.
reflection.question: Think about a moment this week when someone was patient with you. What did it feel like, and did it change how you treated anyone afterward?

readings.label: Second Reading
readings.fullText:
Brothers and sisters:
None of us lives for oneself, and no one dies for oneself.
For if we live, we live for the Lord,
and if we die, we die for the Lord;
so then, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s.
For this is why Christ died and came to life,
that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
readings.summary: Paul is writing to a community in Rome that is wrestling with differences and divisions. He cuts through the noise with something simple: none of us lives or dies for ourselves alone. We belong to Christ, who died and rose so that he could be Lord of everyone. That shared belonging is the reason we treat one another with care.

reflection.reflection: Paul says our lives are not just our own. Everything we do, even the small ordinary things, is connected to something bigger. That can feel like pressure, but it can also feel like company.
reflection.question: When you think about a regular part of your day, like your commute, your work, or how you talk to the people at home, does it feel like something you do alone or something that matters to others too?

readings.label: Gospel
readings.fullText:
Peter approached Jesus and asked him,
“Lord, if my brother sins against me,
how often must I forgive?
As many as seven times?”
Jesus answered, “I say to you, not seven times but seventy-seven times.
That is why the kingdom of heaven may be likened to a king
who decided to settle accounts with his servants.
When he began the accounting,
a debtor was brought before him who owed him a huge amount.
Since he had no way of paying it back,
his master ordered him to be sold,
along with his wife, his children, and all his property,
in payment of the debt.
At that, the servant fell down, did him homage, and said,
‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you back in full.’
Moved with compassion the master of that servant
let him go and forgave him the loan.
When that servant had left, he found one of his fellow servants
who owed him a much smaller amount.
He seized him and started to choke him, demanding,
‘Pay back what you owe.’
Falling to his knees, his fellow servant begged him,
‘Be patient with me, and I will pay you back.’
But he refused.
Instead, he had the fellow servant put in prison
until he paid back the debt.
Now when his fellow servants saw what had happened,
they were deeply disturbed, and went to their master
and reported the whole affair.
His master summoned him and said to him, ‘You wicked servant!
I forgave you your entire debt because you begged me to.
Should you not have had pity on your fellow servant,
as I had pity on you?’
Then in anger his master handed him over to the torturers
until he should pay back the whole debt.
So will my heavenly Father do to you,
unless each of you forgives your brother from your heart.”
readings.summary: Peter thinks he is being generous by offering to forgive someone seven times. Jesus answers with a number so large it is basically saying there is no limit. Then he tells a story about a servant whose master canceled an enormous debt, only to watch that same servant turn around and throw a fellow worker in prison over a small amount. The contrast is meant to land hard. We have been forgiven so much, and Jesus is asking us to let that reality change how we treat others.

reflection.reflection: Jesus is not asking us to pretend a wrong never happened. He is inviting us to notice how much we have already been given and to let that be the starting point for how we respond to others.
reflection.question: Think of a time someone forgave you for something, even something small. How did it affect the way you saw that person or treated them going forward?
